text: A QAOA circuit with badly chosen angles is nearly useless -- Lesson 6 already showed the same circuit swing from a perfect expected cost of 1.0 down to roughly half that from angle choice alone. This lesson covers the classical algorithm outside the quantum computer whose entire job is finding good angles.

Each iteration looks the same. The classical optimizer proposes a candidate gamma and beta. The quantum circuit runs many times at those angles, and the measured bitstrings estimate the expected cost. The optimizer looks at that single number and proposes an improved candidate. Repeat until convergence. The quantum computer never sees the full picture -- it only ever answers 'what's the expected cost at this one point.' All the actual searching happens classically.

Return to the single-edge circuit. At a poor starting point, gamma and beta both 0.1, direct simulation gives an expected cost of only about 0.519. Scanning the full landscape finds the true optimum at gamma about 1.571, beta about 0.393, giving expected cost exactly 1.0. For the larger 4-cycle problem at depth 2, the same style of search -- a coarse grid followed by local refinement -- improved a rough estimate of about 3.932 up to about 3.9998. That refinement, going from good to very close to optimal, is exactly what a classical optimizer contributes.

You might expect gradient descent, but computing an exact gradient would double the number of circuit evaluations per parameter, per iteration, and real hardware measurements are noisy. So many practical implementations instead use gradient-free optimizers -- COBYLA, Nelder-Mead, or SPSA -- which only need the raw cost value, not its derivative, and tend to be more robust to noise. As problem size and depth grow, though, a documented phenomenon called a barren plateau can appear: the cost landscape becomes exponentially flat almost everywhere, and even gradient-free optimizers struggle to find any improving direction at all. This isn't solved; it's active research.

Next lesson asks the natural follow-up question directly: does adding more layers to a QAOA circuit actually help? A direct, exactly-simulated comparison between depth 1 and depth 2 on the same problem answers it.
